tags.description: Flannel, siphon and slow drip: the methods that take their time, and why we still use them.

posts.title: Why we still pour through flannel
posts.excerpt: Cloth is slower than paper, fussier, and has to sleep in the fridge. Forty-seven years in, we would not pour any other way.
posts.content:
Every morning at seven, before the shutters go up, Haruo boils a pan of water and drops in the flannel filters from the day before. They have spent the night in a jar of cold water in the fridge, because flannel must never dry out. A dry filter goes stale, and a stale filter makes stale coffee.

Flannel drip, or nel drip, is the slowest way we know to make a cup. It is also the oldest method at this counter: Michiko poured through cloth on the first day in 1979, and nobody has found a good reason to stop.

Why cloth, not paper

Paper catches almost all of the coffee's oils. Cloth lets some of them through. The result is a heavier, rounder cup, with a texture closer to velvet than water. It is less bright than a paper pour-over, and more forgiving of a dark roast, which is exactly what our house blend is.

Four minutes, give or take

We grind twenty-four grams for each cup, just before pouring. The first few drops of water make the grounds swell and breathe, and then we wait. After thirty seconds the pour begins: a thin stream, the width of a noodle, in small circles that never touch the cloth. We stop before the last drops fall, because the end of a pour is where the bitterness lives.

You cannot rush cloth. It tells you when it is ready, and it is never ready before you are.

Michiko Sato, 1979

Looking after a filter

  • Boil a new filter for ten minutes with a spoon of used grounds before its first use.
  • Rinse in hot water after every pour. Never use soap.
  • Keep it in cold water in the fridge, and change the water daily.
  • Retire it after about a hundred cups, or when the coffee starts to taste of cloth.

If you would like to try at home, we sell the same filters at the counter, and Haruo is happy to show you the pour on a quiet weekday morning. Bring your own kettle if you like. He will probably tell you it is the wrong one, kindly.
